imine2003.title: Proving Correctness of Transformation Functions in Real-Time Groupware
imine2003.author: Abdessamad Imine, Pascal Molli, Gerald Oster, Michael Rusinowitch
imine2003.venue: 8th European Conference on Computer-Supported Cooperative Work (ECSCW'03), Helsinki, Finland, September 2003
imine2003.quote: Proving C1 and C2 on transformation functions is very hard and error prone even on a simple string object. For example, there are 123 different cases to explore when trying to prove C2 on a String object. Each time the specification of transformation functions is changed, it is necessary to redo the proof.
supports: author block on the PDF: 'Abdessamad Imine, Pascal Molli, Gerald Oster and Michael Rusinowitch / ECOO and CASSIS Teams - LORIA France / {imine,molli,oster,rusi}@loria.fr'

abstract: 'To validate our approach, we have verified the correctness of state-of-art transformation functions defined on Strings with surprising results. Counter-examples provided by the theorem prover have helped us to define new correct transformation functions for Strings.'

SPIKE is named in the paper: 'We propose to assist development of transformation functions with SPIKE , an automated theorem prover which is suitable for reasoning about functions defined by conditional rewrite rules'

'This approach requires specifying the transformation functions in first order logic. Then, SPIKE automatically determines the correctness of transformation functions. If correctness is violated, SPIKE returns counter-examples.'
on Ellis and Gibbs' functions: 'SPIKE found the counter-example depicted in figure 3 in a few seconds. SPIKE detected that condition C1 is violated.'
the paper's own proposed functions, later called IMOR: 'This set of transformation functions is correct, w.r.t. C1 and C2 .'
conclusion: 'On a simple String object, each time a function definition changes, you have to explore 123 different cases carefully.'
this 2003 paper writes the two conditions C1 and C2; the 2005 report writes the same two conditions TP1 and TP2

how long the prover takes: 'We express transformation functions using the SPIKE syntax and SPIKE checks conditions in few seconds or few minutes depending of the number of different cases induced by the specification.'
imine2003.note: Read as the authors' PDF (6 pages) hosted on an ENS/LRI course reading list, title, author block and abstract identical to the ECSCW'03 paper. The venue string is taken from the authors' own later citation of it (RR-5795 reference [5]: 'In Proceedings of the 8th European Conference on Computer-Supported Cooperative Work - ECSCW'03, Helsinki, Finland, September 2003.'). The HAL record for the same paper (inria-00107652, queried through the HAL API, which is not behind the site's bot wall) independently gives the title, the four authors and the conference as '8th European Conference of Computer-supported Cooperative Work - ECSCW'03', and lists the deposited version as 18 p. No page range is claimed here; see unverified.

oster2005rr.title: Proving correctness of transformation functions in collaborative editing systems
oster2005rr.author: Gerald Oster, Pascal Urso, Pascal Molli, Abdessamad Imine
oster2005rr.venue: INRIA Research Report RR-5795, Projets ECOO et CASSIS, INRIA Lorraine / LORIA, Nancy
oster2005rr.quote: In this section, we invalidate all previous propositions of transformation functions for string of characters by giving a counter-example for each.
supports: title page: 'Rapport de recherche n 5795 - Decembre 2005 - 45 pages'

section 2: 'Currently, as we demonstrate it in section 4, none transformation functions verifying TP1 and TP2 is known. The problem comes from the huge number of different cases to verify even in case small and simple transformation functions. With an automated theorem prover, we found an error in all existing transformation function.'

conclusion: 'We used automated theorem proving to invalidate all existing transformation functions. These counter-examples leads us to propose the Tombstone Transformation Functions. These functions verifies TP1, TP2.'
section 4 is one subsection per invalidated proposal: 4.1 Ellis's, 4.2 Ressel's, 4.3 IMOR (the authors' own 2003 functions), 4.4 Suleiman's, 4.5 SDT
the prover: 'In our framework, we use the SPIKE [1, 19] automated theorem prover which builds proof by induction.'
abstract: 'Counter-examples provided by the theorem prover helped us to design the tombstone transformation functions.'

section 5, the one shape shared by every counterexample: 'All the transformation functions presented above are designed to manage a very simple tie : three concurrent operations : ins(2, x), del(2) and ins(3, y) ... And all the counter-examples are only instances of this tie. Nevertheless, character b obviously separates x and y.'
section 5, the TTF design: 'Our idea is to keep the deleted character b as a tombstone. This is a transposition of the WOOT approach [16] in the OT framework.'
'If tombstones is a very easy solution for the OT approach, TTF retains a tombstone to mark a deleted character. So, the space overhead of tombstones grows indefinitely.'

reference [16] of RR-5795 is the same authors' 'Real time group editors without operational transformation', Technical Report RR-5580, LORIA-INRIA Lorraine, May 2005 - so WOOT precedes the tombstone transformation functions by seven months rather than following them
how long the prover takes, section 5: 'The complete verification of T P1 and T P2 is totally automatic and takes 1mn30s on a laptop.'
oster2005rr.note: pdftotext renders the subscripts of the two correctness conditions with a space, as 'T P1' and 'T P2'; quoted here as TP1 and TP2. Downloaded from HAL (inria-00071213), which is INRIA's own repository.

oster2005imor.title: Proving correctness of transformation functions in collaborative editing systems, section 4.3 (IMOR transformation functions)
oster2005imor.author: Gerald Oster, Pascal Urso, Pascal Molli, Abdessamad Imine
oster2005imor.quote: In [5], we claimed that this set of transformation functions satisfied TP2. Unfortunately, we made a mistake in the specification of transformation functions.
supports: reference [5] of RR-5795 is the authors' own ECSCW'03 paper, 'Proving Correctness of Transformation Functions in Real-Time Groupware'

the specification bug: 'By specifying p == o as one of the preconditions of operation ins, SPIKE does not generate TP1 or TP2 instances with p != o. However, as presented in figure 13, such a case is possible.'
'We run the prover on this specification and SPIKE returns the counter example presented figure 13.'
Figure 13, 'IMOR counter example (3 sites)': all three sites start on the string 'bcd'; site 2 ends holding 'bxxd' and site 3 ends holding 'bxd'
conclusion: 'Using a theorem prover has some liabilities; it proves what is specified. It does not prevent specification errors. We have done such errors in [5].'
oster2005imor.note: Same document as oster2005rr, kept as a separate key so the self-refutation facts and the field-wide facts cite different sections. Subscripts normalised as above; the '!=' in the specification-bug quote is a rendered mathematical not-equals.

woot2006.title: Data Consistency for P2P Collaborative Editing
woot2006.author: Gerald Oster, Pascal Urso, Pascal Molli, Abdessamad Imine
woot2006.venue: ACM Conference on Computer-Supported Cooperative Work, CSCW'06, November 4-8, 2006, Banff, Alberta, Canada, pp. 259-268
woot2006.quote: However, WOOT retains tombstones to record deleted characters. So, the space overhead of tombstones grows indefinitely.
supports: HAL citation line on the deposited PDF: 'ACM Conference on Computer-Supported Cooperative Work - CSCW 2006, Nov 2006, Banff, Alberta, Canada, pp.259 - 268.'; the paper's own copyright block reads 'CSCW'06, November 4-8, 2006, Banff, Alberta, Canada.'
'Since our definitions of operation are based on elements rather than positions, the elements are uniquely identified.'

'Definition 3. A character identifier is a pair (ns, ng) where ns is the identifier of a site and ng is a natural number.' ... 'Since numSite is unique, this pair forms a unique identifier for a character.'

'Definition 1. A W-character c is a five-tuple < id, a, v, idcp, idcn >' with id the character's identifier, a the alphabetical value, v a visibility flag, and idcp / idcn the identifiers of the previous and next W-characters

'We reuse the approach of "death certificates" or "tombstones" used in Usenet. If an element is deleted we maintain useful informations about it but not its whole content. For a character, it is equivalent to make the character invisible.'
insert names neighbours, not a position: Figure 1 gives the WOOT operation as 'ins(a<1<b)' against the position-based 'ins(2,'1')'

'In summary, WOOT is an optimistic replication algorithm that ensures convergence and intention preservation. It requires no vector clocks contrary to most operational transformation based algorithms.'

the paper's stated motivation for dropping transformation is P2P scale, not TP2: 'Clearly, vectors clocks prevent these algorithms to scale and represent a serious bottleneck for their deployment on P2P networks.'

tombstone GC is left open: 'We can use an expiration period for garbaging deleted characters but this method is unsafe. We can also use a two-phase protocol to purge safely the tombstones as in [19] but all sites must be alive for the algorithm to make progress.'

the CSCW 2006 page range is confirmed a second time from outside HAL, by Shapiro et al. 2011 reference [30]: 'Data consistency for P2P collaborative editing. In Int. Conf. on Computer-Supported Coop. Work (CSCW), pages 259-268, Banff, Alberta, Canada, November 2006. ACM Press.'
woot2006.note: WOOT appeared first as INRIA Research Report RR-5580, 'Real time group editors without Operational transformation', Oster, Urso, Molli, Imine, cover page 'N 5580 - Mai 2005', 24 pages (HAL inria-00071240) - verified from that report's cover page only; its body has a corrupt text layer and nothing from it is quoted. The 2006 date used here is the CSCW publication, and the prose makes no claim about which of WOOT and TTF came first beyond RR-5795's own statement that TTF transposes WOOT.

shapiro2011.title: A comprehensive study of Convergent and Commutative Replicated Data Types
shapiro2011.author: Marc Shapiro, Nuno Preguica, Carlos Baquero, Marek Zawirski
shapiro2011.quote: It is inspired by WOOT, a CRDT for concurrent editing [30].
supports: 'Thus, the WOOT data structure for concurrent editing corresponds directly to the Add-Remove Partial Order of Specification 18.'

the survey's definition of the text type: 'A sequence for text editing (or just sequence hereafter) is a totally-ordered set of elements, each composed of a unique identifier and an atom (e.g., a character, a string, an XML tag, or an embedded graphic), supporting operations to add an element at some position, and to remove an element.'
the survey covers RGA and Treedoc as sequence CRDTs in the same section
shapiro2011.note: Used only for the retrospective naming: WOOT predates the term CRDT (2006 vs 2011) and this is the paper that files it under the name.

unverified: The page range of the ECSCW'03 paper. DBLP lists 'Proving Correctness of Transformation Functions in Real-Time Groupware', pages 276-293, in the Springer proceedings; the copy actually opened is the authors' 6-page PDF and carries no page numbers. No page range for that paper appears in the prose or on a card. Both HAL (inria-00107652) and the Springer chapter page refused automated access.

Any claim that the counterexamples caused the authors to abandon operational transformation. The sequence is documented - the same four names, RR-5795 in December 2005 and WOOT at CSCW 2006 - but the WOOT paper gives peer-to-peer scale and the cost of vector clocks as its motivation, and never cites TP2 failure as the reason. The prose states the order of events and the shared mechanism, not a motive.

Ellis and Gibbs, 'Concurrency Control in Groupware Systems', ACM SIGMOD 1989 - the origin of operational transformation and of the first transformation functions. Confirmed only as reference [3] in RR-5795 and reference [7] in the WOOT paper; four public copies of the PDF returned HTML error pages, so the paper was never opened. Neither Ellis, Gibbs nor 1989 appears in the prose.
What any of this cost in money. These are research papers; no budget, headcount or dollar figure is printed in any of them, and none is claimed here.

The line of descent from WOOT to Yjs and Automerge. Shapiro et al. 2011 names WOOT as a CRDT and defines the sequence type by unique identifiers, but no source opened here documents a direct influence on the modern libraries, and none is claimed.
